mcqs.question: What does React do first when state changes, before it touches the real DOM?
options: It patches the real DOM immediately for the changed component only
It calls a Proxy layer to detect exactly which value changed
It re-runs the component function to build a new virtual-DOM tree, then diffs it against the previous one
It skips rendering entirely if no signal was explicitly declared
mcqs.explanation: React re-runs the render function unconditionally on a state change, producing a new virtual tree, and only after diffing that tree against the previous one does it touch the real DOM — and only for the parts that actually differ. There's no Proxy-based value tracking in React's own model.

mcqs.question: In a fine-grained, signal-based framework, what registers a piece of UI as a subscriber to a signal?
options: Explicitly calling a `subscribe()` function inside every component
Wrapping the component in a `memo()` call
Declaring the signal at the top of the file
Reading the signal's current value inside a reactive scope, such as a template expression
mcqs.explanation: Subscription happens automatically the moment a reactive value is read inside a tracked scope — the framework records that read as a dependency, no explicit subscribe call needed. Just declaring a signal without reading it anywhere creates no subscribers at all.

mcqs.question: Per the comparison table, what's the main manual step React developers take that fine-grained frameworks usually don't need?
options: Applying `memo`/`useMemo`/`useCallback` to skip unnecessary re-renders
Manually diffing the previous and next DOM trees by hand
Writing explicit subscribe/unsubscribe calls for every piece of state
Declaring which DOM nodes exist before rendering begins
mcqs.explanation: Because React doesn't track dependencies automatically, avoiding wasted re-renders is a manual opt-out via memoization APIs. Fine-grained frameworks already know the precise dependency, so most of that manual work isn't needed — diffing itself is automatic in React, not something developers do by hand.

mcqs.question: Why can fine-grained reactivity skip the diffing step that virtual-DOM frameworks rely on?
options: Because it doesn't support conditional rendering
Because the dependency graph is already known from tracking reads at setup time, so there's nothing left to discover by comparison
Because it re-renders every component on every state change instead
Because diffing is only required for server-rendered pages
mcqs.explanation: Diffing exists solely to discover what changed after the fact; fine-grained reactivity records that information up front when a value is read, so there's no tree to build or compare later — the update goes straight to the exact subscriber. It doesn't re-render more, it renders less.

mcqs.question: Which statement about virtual DOM usage across frameworks is accurate?
options: Svelte uses a virtual DOM identical to React's
SolidJS re-renders its whole component function on every signal update, like React
Vue 3 uses a virtual DOM internally, but its fine-grained reactivity can skip re-rendering subtrees a signal doesn't affect
All frameworks that use JSX must use a virtual DOM
mcqs.explanation: Vue is a genuine hybrid: it keeps a virtual DOM but layers Proxy-based fine-grained tracking on top to avoid unnecessary subtree re-renders. Svelte has no virtual DOM at all, SolidJS components run once rather than re-rendering, and JSX is just syntax — SolidJS uses JSX without a virtual DOM.
